source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009)

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: The first part of community diagnosis, considered the "keystone" of the community health nursing process, is:
questions.rationale: Community assessment collects and analyzes data on factors influencing the population's health.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Community diagnosis (PDF p. 152)
questions.quote: This is the first part of the community diagnostic process called the community assessment and is considered to be the "keystone" of community health nursing process.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: After a sudden dengue outbreak in a barangay, the PHN should conduct which type of community diagnosis?
questions.rationale: A problem-oriented assessment focuses on a specific problem such as an outbreak or disaster; comprehensive assessment gathers general information.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Types of community diagnosis (PDF p. 153)
questions.quote: Oftentimes, the nurse is confronted with a specific problem area like a disaster situation or an outbreak of disease. In these instances, a problem-oriented assessment will have to be conducted.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A newly assigned PHN drives around the barangay to get a quick feel of its houses, roads and people before planning the community diagnosis. This is a:
questions.rationale: A rapid appraisal by ocular or windshield survey gives a bird's-eye view before the actual community diagnosis.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Collecting the data (PDF p. 160)
questions.quote: A common approach is to perform a rapid appraisal through an ocular survey or what others call as windshield survey.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: The nurse uses barangay records of births and deaths compiled by the municipal health office. These are:
questions.rationale: Secondary data are existing data collected by others; primary data are collected directly by the nurse for the objectives.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Determining the data (PDF p. 159)
questions.quote: Secondary data are existing data that were obtained by other people which the nurse can use

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: To learn about the barangay's health programs, the nurse interviews the barangay kagawad for health. This method is a:
questions.rationale: A key informant interview targets a person who is an expert or authority on the subject.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Interviews (PDF p. 161)
questions.quote: When a person to be an expert or an authority on a specific subject is interviewed, this is known as the Key Informant Interview (KII).

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: In the census, a seaman is counted in his hometown even though he is abroad on census day. This is the:
questions.rationale: De jure assigns people to their usual residence; de facto assigns them where they are physically present on census day.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Demography (PDF p. 180)
questions.quote: The de jure method is done when people are assigned to the place where they usually live regardless of where they are at the time of the census.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Births, deaths and marriages recorded by the local civil registrar are sources of demographic data called:
questions.rationale: Registration systems record vital events such as births, deaths and marriages.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Sources of demographic data (PDF p. 181)
questions.quote: Registration systems such that collected by the civil registrar's office deal with recording of vital events in the community.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A barangay has 520 males and 480 females. The sex ratio is about:
questions.rationale: Sex ratio = males ÷ females × 100 = 520 ÷ 480 × 100 ≈ 108 males per 100 females.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Population composition (PDF p. 182)
questions.quote: The sex ratio represents the number of males for every 100 females in the population.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A town has 3,000 people aged 0–14, 500 aged 65 and above, and 5,000 aged 15–64. The dependency ratio is:
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Dependency ratio (PDF p. 182)
questions.quote: The dependency ratio represents the number of economically dependent for every 100 economically productive.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A population pyramid with a broad base and narrow top shows a population that is:
questions.rationale: The youngest age group is the base bar; a wide base means many children and high fertility.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Population pyramid (PDF p. 183)
questions.quote: The first bar represents the youngest age group and drawn at the base of the pyramid.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A family of 8 sleeps in 2 rooms. The crowding index is:
questions.rationale: Crowding index = persons in household ÷ rooms used for sleeping = 8 ÷ 2 = 4; high crowding eases disease spread.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Population distribution (PDF p. 185)
questions.quote: Crowding index is described by dividing the num o persons m a household with the number of rooms used by the family for sleeping.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A municipality with a midyear population of 40,000 had 920 live births. The crude birth rate is:
questions.rationale: CBR = live births ÷ midyear population × 1,000 = 920 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000 = 23.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 185)
questions.quote: number of live births - x 1000 midyear population

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: The denominator of the general fertility rate is the midyear population of:
questions.rationale: General fertility rate = live births ÷ midyear population of women 15–44 × 1,000.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 186)
questions.quote: midyear population of women, 15-44 years of age

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A town recorded 600 live births and 12 deaths of infants under 1 year. The infant mortality rate is:
questions.rationale: IMR = deaths under 1 year ÷ live births × 1,000 = 12 ÷ 600 × 1,000 = 20.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 186)
questions.quote: deaths under one year of age - x 1000 number of live births

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: The denominator used for maternal mortality is the number of:
questions.rationale: Maternal deaths (pregnancy, delivery, puerperium) are divided by live births; today it is usually expressed per 100,000 live births.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 186)
questions.quote: number of deaths due to pregnancy, delivery and puerperium Maternal Mortality Rate = - number of live births

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A measure of the overall health of a population that gives the percentage of deaths occurring at age 50 and above is the:
questions.rationale: Swaroop's index = deaths among those 50 and over ÷ total deaths × 100; a high value suggests good health status.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 187)
questions.quote: number of deaths among those 50 years and over - x 100 Swaroop's Index = - total deaths

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Of 40 diagnosed rabies cases in a province, 40 died. The case fatality rate is:
questions.rationale: CFR = deaths from a disease ÷ cases of that disease × 100 = 40 ÷ 40 × 100 = 100%.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Vital statistics (PDF p. 187)
questions.quote: number of deaths from a specified cause - x 100 number of cases of the same disease

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Which rate counts both old and new cases of a disease at a given time?
questions.rationale: Prevalence includes old and new cases; incidence counts only new cases among the population at risk.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Morbidity rates (PDF p. 186)
questions.quote: number of old and new cases of a disease population examined

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Of 120 guests who ate at a fiesta, 30 developed diarrhea within a day. The attack rate is:
questions.rationale: Attack rate = new cases ÷ population at risk (exposed) × 100 = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25%.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Descriptive epidemiology (PDF p. 195)
questions.quote: It represents the incidence of the illness among the exposed population.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: In the ecologic triad of disease causation, the three elements are agent, host and:
questions.rationale: The ecologic triad stresses the interaction of agent, host and environment; a change in any one disturbs equilibrium.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Multiple causation (PDF p. 187)
questions.quote: the ecologic triad is most helpful to the nurse because it highlights not only the host's and agent's roles in disease development but also regards the role of the environment

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Lack of iodine causing goiter is an example of which type of agent?
questions.rationale: Nutritive agents include iron or iodine deficiency and cholesterol; biological agents are microorganisms.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Agent types (PDF p. 188)
questions.quote: iron or iodine deficiency, cholesterol

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Immunizing children against measles is which level of prevention?
questions.rationale: Primary prevention includes health promotion and specific protection (immunization, chemoprophylaxis).
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Levels of prevention (PDF p. 189)
questions.quote: Specific measures include provision of immunization and prophylaxis to vulnerable or at-risk groups

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A blood pressure screening drive in the barangay hall is which level of prevention?
questions.rationale: Secondary prevention identifies and treats problems early: screening, case finding, prompt treatment.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Levels of prevention (PDF p. 189)
questions.quote: Such interventions include screening, case finding, disease surveillance, prompt and appropriate treatment.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A sheltered workshop for clients recovering from mental illness is an example of:
questions.rationale: Tertiary prevention limits disability and rehabilitates, e.g., day care centers and sheltered workshops.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Levels of prevention (PDF p. 190)
questions.quote: Day care centers and sheltered workshops are examples of opportunities to achieve the objective of tertiary prevention in mental illness and drug abuse.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: In the natural history of disease, the stage when risk factors are present but disease has not developed is:
questions.rationale: Prepathogenesis (susceptibility): factors favoring disease are present but disease has not developed.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Natural history of disease (PDF p. 189)
questions.quote: Prepathogenesis or susceptibility — in this stage, disease has not developed but factors that favor its occurrence are present.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Screening tests differ from diagnostic tests because screening:
options: Is only a preliminary step to diagnosis
Is done only on sick people
questions.rationale: Screening presumptively identifies unrecognized disease in apparently well people; confirmation is still needed.
explanations: Meant to be rapid and cheap.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Descriptive epidemiology (PDF p. 193)
questions.quote: It is NOT a diagnostic measure but a preliminary step to diagnosis.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Malaria is always present at a low, steady level in some upland provinces. This pattern is:
questions.rationale: Endemic means habitual presence of disease in an area; epidemic is a marked rise; sporadic is occasional scattered cases.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Descriptive epidemiology (PDF p. 195)
questions.quote: An endemic occurrence of disease implies the habitual presence of disease in a given geographic location

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Many guests fall ill within hours after eating contaminated food at the same party. This is a:
questions.rationale: Common-source epidemics result from simultaneous exposure to one source; propagated epidemics spread person to person.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Time pattern (PDF p. 196)
questions.quote: Common source epidemic is characterized by simultaneous exposure of a large number of susceptible to a common infectious agent

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Lung cancer incidence is 2.0 per 1,000 among heavy smokers and 0.1 per 1,000 among nonsmokers. The relative risk is:
questions.rationale: Relative risk = incidence in exposed ÷ incidence in unexposed = 2.0 ÷ 0.1 = 20; smokers have 20 times the risk.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Risk estimates (PDF p. 197)
questions.quote: Incidence Rate among those exposed Relative Risk Ratio - Incidence Rate among those not exposed

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A relative risk of 1.0 means that:
options: Exposure does not change the risk
questions.rationale: RR of 1.0 means equal risk in exposed and unexposed; above 1.0 means excess risk in the exposed.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Risk estimates (PDF p. 196)
questions.quote: A relative risk ratio of 1.0 means that the risk is the same for both exposed and non- exposed populations.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: In a case-control study, which measure of association is used because incidence cannot be computed?
questions.rationale: Case-control studies start with disease status, so the odds ratio (ad/bc) estimates risk.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Analytic study designs (PDF p. 199)
questions.quote: The incidence or prevalence rate can not be computed in case-control study design; hence, the odds ratio will be the

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: The branch of epidemiology that describes disease by person, place and time is:
questions.rationale: Descriptive epidemiology deals with frequency and distribution; analytical tests hypotheses on causes.
questions.source: Maglaya, Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th ed. (2009), Ch. 7 Epidemiological approach (PDF p. 193)
questions.quote: Descriptive Epidemiology concerned with disease distribution and frequency
